added_claim_errors: United's credits usually run about a year from the original ticket date: unverifiable claim about United's own policy, and beside the point because a credit in lieu of a refund must last 5 years.
A plain one year can come up short, so asks for 12 months from today: builds the draft around a one-year term that is below the legal minimum of 5 years; misleading framing.
Summary link from komonews.com is offered as the rule's source; it is a secondary news summary and I did not open it (unverified).

United's credits often run about 12 months from the original ticket date, and some require you to fly before the expiry rather than just book: unverifiable claim about United's policy, and the draft asks for only 12 months instead of the 5 years the rule requires.
The credit should include taxes and fees: plausible but not covered by the key and not sourced.

reasons: Both answers open by correcting the agent. Both say a weather cancellation still gives a cash refund if the passenger declines the rebooking, and that weather only removes hotel and meal obligations. Both then draft the message accepting a one-year credit, which the key lists as a deduction. Neither mentions the 5-year minimum for a credit offered in lieu of a refund. B states the 7-business-day card refund deadline, says the refund goes to the original form of payment, cites the Federal Register final rule (89 FR 32760, which I recall from my own knowledge and did not open), and tells the person how to edit the letter into a refund request. A hedges more ("very likely", "generally treated", "Your call"), gives no deadline, and only offers to write the refund version later. A is slightly shorter, but B covers more of the key points and gives the more usable correction, so B wins.
